'''Sir Robert Forsyth Scott''' (28 July 1849 &ndash; 18 November 1933) was a [[mathematician]], [[barrister]] and Master of [[St John's College, Cambridge]]

==Life==
Scott was born in [[Leith]], near [[Edinburgh]], the eldest son of Reverend George Scott, a Minister in the church at [[Dairsie]] and Mary Forsyth, daughter of the Edinburgh advocate Robert Forsyth.<ref name = "Biog">[http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Scott_Robert.html Biography of Robert Forsyth Scott]</ref>

Scott was educated at the High School, Edinburgh, then in [[Stuttgart]] before becoming a student at [[University College, London]]. In 1870, while a student at University College, London, he was awarded a Whitworth Exhibition. He went on to read mathematics at St John's College, where he was fourth [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] in the [[Tripos]] in 1875 and was elected to a fellowship in 1877.<ref>{{acad|id=SCT871RF|name=Scott, Robert Forsyth}}</ref><ref name = "histecon">[http://www-histecon.kings.cam.ac.uk/research/digitization/rfscott.html Digitization of History: Centre for History and Economics]</ref>

After publishing ''The Theory of Determinants and Their Applications'' in 1880, Scott turned his attention to the law,  become a [[barrister]] in 1883, and to institutional history, including histories of St. John's College, Cambridge, published between 1882 and 1907.<ref name = "Biog"/><ref name = "histecon"/>
In 1908 he was appointed as the Master of St John's College, a position he held until his death in [[Cambridge]] in 1933, and from 1910 to 1912 he served as [[List of Vice-Chancellors of the University of Cambridge|Vice-chancellor of the University]].  On his death he left the library of St John's one of the largest collection of [[Burma|Burmese]] manuscripts in [[Europe]].<ref name = "histecon"/>

He was the elder brother of Sir [[James George Scott]].

==Publications==
* ''[https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/27320 History of St John's College, Cambridge]''
* ''[https://digital.library.cornell.edu/cgi/t/text/text-idx?c=math;cc=math;view=toc;subview=short;idno=01670002 The theory of determinants and their applications]'' (2nd ed., revised by [[George Ballard Mathews]]), Cambridge University Press, 1904.
